t1: Write a Python function `def sum_positive_evens(numbers: list) -> int` that returns the sum of all positive even integers in the list.
t2: Also skip any values in the list that are not integers (e.g., strings, floats, None, booleans) instead of raising an error.
t3: If the resulting sum is 0 (no qualifying numbers found), return -1 instead of 0.

t1: Write a Python function `def is_palindrome_alnum(s: str) -> bool` that returns True if the string is a palindrome when considering only alphanumeric characters, case-insensitively (all other characters are ignored).
t2: Ensure that a string which becomes empty after filtering out non-alphanumeric characters returns True.
t3: Additionally, treat the underscore character '_' as a kept character in the comparison (i.e., include underscores alongside alphanumeric characters, still case-insensitive), rather than discarding it.

t1: Write a Python function `def flatten_and_dedupe(nested: list) -> list` that flattens a list that may contain nested lists (of arbitrary depth) of integers, and returns a list of unique integers preserving first-occurrence order.
t2: Also ignore (skip) any non-integer values found anywhere in the nested structure (e.g. strings, None, floats, booleans) instead of raising errors.
t3: Return the result sorted in descending order instead of preserving first-occurrence order.

t1: Write a Python function `def word_frequency_top_n(text: str, n: int) -> list` that lowercases text, splits on whitespace, strips punctuation characters (any character in string.punctuation) from each token, and returns the top n most frequent words as a list of (word, count) tuples, ordered by count descending.
t2: For ties in count, break ties alphabetically ascending, so the result order is fully deterministic.
t3: Exclude the following stopwords from consideration entirely (they must never appear in the output, and don't count toward any word's frequency): {'the','a','an','and','or','of','to','in'}.
tests:
def test_basic():
    text = "The cat sat on the mat. The cat was happy."
    result = word_frequency_top_n(text, 2)
    assert result == [("cat", 2), ("happy", 1)]
def test_tie_alphabetical():
    text = "dog cat bird"
    result = word_frequency_top_n(text, 3)
    assert result == [("bird",1), ("cat",1), ("dog",1)]
def test_stopwords_excluded():
    text = "the a an and or of to in dog dog cat"
    result = word_frequency_top_n(text, 5)
    assert result == [("dog", 2), ("cat", 1)]
def test_punctuation_stripped():
    text = "Hello, hello! HELLO."
    result = word_frequency_top_n(text, 1)
    assert result == [("hello", 3)]

t1: Write a Python function `def caesar_cipher(text: str, shift: int) -> str` that shifts each alphabetic character by `shift` positions (wrapping within its case a-z / A-Z), leaving non-alphabetic characters unchanged.
t2: Support negative shift values correctly (shifting backward), and normalize any shift value outside -25..25 using modulo 26 first.
t3: Add a `decode` parameter with default False: the signature becomes `def caesar_cipher(text: str, shift: int, decode: bool = False) -> str`. When `decode=True`, apply the inverse shift (equivalent to calling with -shift and decode=False).

t1: Write a Python function `def run_length_encode(s: str) -> str` implementing run-length encoding: consecutive repeated characters become '<count><char>' (e.g. 'aaab' -> '3a1b'). A run of exactly 1 is still printed with an explicit '1' prefix at this stage.
t2: Handle the empty string input by returning an empty string.
t3: Change the output format so a run of exactly 1 is printed as just the character with no leading '1' (e.g. 'aaab' -> '3ab' instead of '3a1b'), while runs of 2 or more keep the numeric count prefix.

t1: Write a Python function `def matrix_transpose(matrix: list) -> list` that returns the transpose of a rectangular matrix given as a list of lists of numbers.
t2: Raise `ValueError` if the input rows are not all the same length (a ragged matrix).
t3: Support an empty matrix (`[]`) as input by returning `[]`.

t1: Write a Python function `def valid_parentheses(s: str) -> bool` that returns True if all brackets of types (), [], {} in the string are balanced and properly nested. Ignore all other characters.
t2: Return False if the string contains no bracket characters at all (an empty bracket set counts as invalid for this task).
t3: Add support for angle brackets <> as a fourth bracket type that must also be balanced and properly nested (interleaved correctly with the other three types).

t1: Write a Python function `def chunk_list(items: list, size: int) -> list` that splits `items` into consecutive chunks (sublists) of length `size`, with the last chunk possibly shorter.
t2: Raise `ValueError` if `size` is less than or equal to 0.
t3: Add a `fill=None` keyword parameter: the signature becomes `def chunk_list(items: list, size: int, fill=None) -> list`. If `fill` is not None, pad the last chunk with the fill value so every chunk has exactly `size` elements.

t1: Write a Python function `def fizzbuzz_custom(n: int) -> list` returning a list of strings for integers 1..n inclusive: 'Fizz' if divisible by 3, 'Buzz' if divisible by 5, 'FizzBuzz' if divisible by both, else the number as a string.
t2: Handle n=0 or negative n by returning an empty list.
t3: Add a third rule: numbers divisible by 7 append 'Bazz' to whatever was already produced (so a number divisible by 3 and 7 gives 'FizzBazz', by 5 and 7 gives 'BuzzBazz', by 3, 5 and 7 gives 'FizzBuzzBazz', and by 7 alone gives 'Bazz').

t1: Write a Python function `def dedupe_preserve_order(items: list) -> list` returning a list with duplicate elements removed, keeping only the first occurrence, preserving original order. Elements are hashable (may be a mix of strings and other hashable types).
t2: Make deduplication case-insensitive specifically for string elements (i.e., 'Cat' and 'cat' are considered duplicates of each other; keep whichever casing was seen first). Non-string elements are compared as before.
t3: For this final version, assume all inputs are strings. Return the deduped list (still case-insensitive dedup, first-seen casing kept) sorted alphabetically in a case-insensitive manner, instead of in first-occurrence order.

t1: Write a Python function `def binary_search_insert(sorted_list: list, target) -> int` using binary search that returns the index at which `target` should be inserted into `sorted_list` (an ascending-sorted list of comparable items) to keep it sorted, matching Python's `bisect.bisect_left` behavior when `target` is not already present.
t2: If `target` already exists in the list (one or more times), insert after the last occurrence instead (i.e., match `bisect.bisect_right` behavior).
t3: Add support for descending-sorted input lists: if `sorted_list` is sorted in descending order (length >= 2 and first element > last element), return the index that keeps the list sorted descending after inserting `target` (equal targets are inserted after the last occurrence of an equal value, mirroring the bisect_right rule but for descending order).

t1: Write a Python function `def temperature_convert(value: float, from_unit: str, to_unit: str) -> float` supporting units 'C', 'F', 'K' converting between Celsius, Fahrenheit, and Kelvin. Round the result to 2 decimal places.
t2: Raise `ValueError` for any unit (from_unit or to_unit) not in {'C','F','K'}.
t3: Add support for lowercase unit inputs ('c','f','k') by normalizing units to uppercase before processing (mixed case such as 'c' to 'F' must also work).

t1: Write a Python function `def anagram_groups(words: list) -> list` that groups words that are anagrams of each other (case-insensitive), returning a list of lists. Each inner list contains the original-cased words belonging to that group in input order. Groups are ordered by the position of the first word that started that group.
t2: Strip leading/trailing whitespace from each word before comparison (but keep the original including any internal formatting in the output).
t3: Exclude groups that contain only a single word (i.e., words with no anagram partner elsewhere in the input) from the final output.

t1: Write a Python function `def roman_to_int(s: str) -> int` converting a valid uppercase Roman numeral string (using standard subtractive notation, e.g. 'IX'=9, 'MCMXCIV'=1994) to an integer.
t2: Raise `ValueError` if the string contains any character outside 'IVXLCDM'.
t3: Also accept lowercase Roman numerals (and mixed case) by normalizing the string to uppercase before validation and conversion.

t1: Write a Python function `def moving_average(values: list, window: int) -> list` returning a list of the simple moving average (float) over consecutive windows of size `window` (result length = len(values) - window + 1). Assume 1 <= window <= len(values) for this initial version.
t2: Raise `ValueError` if `window` is less than 1 or greater than `len(values)`.
t3: Round each average in the result to 3 decimal places.

t1: Write a Python function `def merge_intervals(intervals: list) -> list` where `intervals` is a list of [start, end] integer pairs; merge all overlapping intervals and return the merged list sorted by start ascending. Intervals only touching at the boundary (e.g. [1,3] and [3,5]) should be merged at this stage.
t2: Handle an empty input list by returning an empty list.
t3: Change the merge rule so that intervals only touching at the boundary (end of one equals start of the next) are NOT merged — only intervals that strictly overlap (share more than a single boundary point) are merged. For example [1,3] and [3,5] must remain as two separate intervals in the output.

t1: Write a Python function `def parse_query_string(qs: str) -> dict` that parses a URL query string like 'a=1&b=2&c=3' (no leading '?') into a dict of string keys to string values.
t2: Support repeated keys by collecting all values for that key into a list, in the order they appear (e.g. 'a=1&a=2' -> {'a': ['1','2']}); keys that appear exactly once remain a plain string value (not wrapped in a list).
t3: URL-decode percent-encoded sequences and treat '+' as a space in both keys and values, using the decoding rules of `urllib.parse.unquote_plus`.

t1: Write a Python function `def histogram_bucket(values: list, bucket_size: int) -> dict` that buckets non-negative integers into ranges of width `bucket_size` starting at 0 (e.g. bucket_size=10: 0-9, 10-19, ...), returning a dict mapping bucket start (int) to the count of values in that bucket. Only include buckets that have at least one value.
t2: Raise `ValueError` if any value in `values` is negative.
t3: Return the dict with keys iterated in ascending sorted order by bucket start (still only a plain dict, but constructed/iterated so ascending order is guaranteed, e.g. via a sorted dict construction).

t1: Write a Python function `def levenshtein_distance(a: str, b: str) -> int` computing the standard Levenshtein edit distance (insertions, deletions, and substitutions each cost 1) between strings `a` and `b`.
t2: Make the comparison case-insensitive (treat 'A' and 'a' as equal, no substitution cost between them).
t3: Change the substitution cost to 2 instead of 1 (insertions and deletions remain cost 1 each), and recompute distances accordingly under this new cost model.
